title: Poultry farm records and administrative processes, at

lessons.title: Production and flock records
lessons.html:
Why records matter

Records are the memory of the farm. They show how each flock performed, prove that animal health and food safety rules were followed and give the information needed for decisions and payments. Customers, abattoirs, auditors and the state vet may ask to see them.

Flock records

Each flock should have its own record file or system entry, starting at placement:

  • flock number, house, breed, hatchery, date placed and number placed
  • daily mortality and culls, with reasons where known
  • daily feed delivered and used, and water meter readings
  • minimum and maximum temperature and humidity
  • weekly body weights and uniformity
  • egg production, grades and floor eggs for layers and breeders
  • lighting programme changes
  • depletion date, number and weight sent to the abattoir or market

Health and medicine records

Keep a vaccination and treatment register: date, product, batch number, dose method, who gave it and, for medicines, the withdrawal period from the label or vet. Products must be used according to the label, as required for registered products under Act 36 of 1947 or by your vet's prescription. Birds or eggs must not go to market before the withdrawal period ends. Keep post-mortem and laboratory reports with the flock file.

Biosecurity records

  • visitors' register
  • vehicle disinfection log
  • rodent bait station checks
  • cleaning and disinfection checklists between flocks
  • water test results

Good recording habits

  1. Record at the same time each day.
  2. Write clearly in pen, or enter data in the farm app the same day.
  3. Never change a figure without crossing out neatly, initialling and dating.
  4. Check the house sheets weekly and transfer totals to the flock summary.
  5. Store records safely and keep them for the period your company or customers require.

lessons.title: Administrative processes: stock, orders and reporting
lessons.html:
The admin behind production

Behind every flock is paperwork: orders, deliveries, stock counts, timesheets and reports. A supervisor who handles admin well prevents shortages, stops losses and makes sure people and suppliers are paid correctly.

Ordering and receiving

Order chicks, feed, vaccines, litter, gas and disinfectant through the farm's approved process, usually a requisition signed by the manager and a purchase order. When goods arrive:

  1. Check the delivery note against the order: product, quantity, batch and expiry date.
  2. Inspect quality, for example torn feed bags, wet shavings, or vaccines not kept cold.
  3. Sign only for what you received and note any shortages on the delivery note.
  4. File the delivery note and pass a copy to the office for payment.

Stock control

Keep stock cards or a stock system for the feed store, chemicals store and vaccine fridge. Record every receipt and every issue. Do a physical count at least monthly and compare with the records. Investigate differences. Store chemicals locked and away from feed, and record the fridge temperature daily for vaccines.

People admin

Keep daily attendance or timesheets, overtime records and leave forms. Hand them in on time so wages are correct. Record injuries in the incident register and report them as the farm procedure requires.

Reports

Prepare short weekly reports for the manager: placements, mortality, feed and water use, weights or egg production against standard, problems and actions. At depletion, prepare a flock summary with liveability, FCR or eggs per hen and costs. Use the farm's template so reports can be compared.

Using a farm system

Many farms now capture data on a phone or tablet. Enter data the same day, check for typing errors, and back up or sync regularly. Never share your login.

Key points

  • Every flock needs complete production, health and biosecurity records.
  • Record medicine batch numbers and respect withdrawal periods from the label or vet.
  • Check deliveries against orders before signing.
  • Keep stock cards and count stock regularly.
  • Submit timesheets and weekly reports on time using farm templates.
